transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28 15:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Lucas Patel, Erin Soto (Redwood) — Rajiv Menon, Alyssa Greene, Tom Brooks (Quasar Labs)

Summary: quick discovery and POC scoping to validate per-token economics for a user-assist feature. Goal: decide whether hosted API can meet latency/cost targets or if dedicated/VPC pilot needed.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with lucas our se and erin on success. how's everyone doing?
00:42 Rajiv Menon: hey, doing good, thanks. busy quarter but excited to dig in.
01:05 Alyssa Greene: hi — Alyssa here. we wanted to focus today on cost modeling and a benchmark plan, plus any security constraints that would effect the pilot.
01:30 Lucas Patel: great. quick agenda: first, understand your workload shape and success criteria; second, walk through per-token math and batching / caching levers; third, scope a 24-72 hour benchmark and timeline. does that sound right?
02:10 Tom Brooks: yep that's perfect. we have a hard budget for phase one, about $40-50k/month, and we need p95 latency under 400ms for interactive flows.
03:05 Maya Chen: ok good — that budget and latency are reasonable to aim at. can you tell us about traffic patterns? tokens per request, concurrency, and average session length?
03:40 Rajiv Menon: typical prompt is around 120 tokens in, and we generate like 200 tokens out on average for the assistant feature. concurrency peaks around 250 qps but most sustained is 40-60 qps, daily average lower.
04:20 Alyssa Greene: also worth noting many requests reuse the same prefix prompts per user flow, so caching could help.
05:00 Lucas Patel: that's helpful — with prefix caching and batching you can often reduce effective tokens billed by 20-40% depending on reuse. for modeling i'll show two scenarios: hosted with heavy caching, and dedicated reserved capacity with larger batch sizes.
05:45 Rajiv Menon: one question — how do you account for KV cache storage and TTLs? we have stateful prefixes per user session.
06:20 Lucas Patel: we model prefix/KV caching as a reduction in repeated token decode work; e.g., if 30% of tokens are cache hits, you get a direct token-bill reduction minus a small cache-store cost for memory. in Redwood Dedicated you can pin long-lived KV caches which improves hit rate; hosted also supports prefix caching with similar SLOs.
07:10 Tom Brooks: ok, what about quantization? we run smaller models for some paths but need quality to stay high.
07:45 Lucas Patel: quantization (8-bit, 4-bit) reduces GPU compute and cost significantly, we provide recommendations per model. for quality-sensitive flows we'd A/B test quantized variants during bench.
08:25 Alyssa Greene: can you give a back-of-envelope per-token number so we can check against budget?
08:50 Maya Chen: sure — let's run a rough calc live. scenario A: hosted, mix of 120 in + 200 out = 320 tokens per request. at 60 qps sustained (5.18M requests/day) — wait that's wrong — lucas, quick sanity check —
09:35 Lucas Patel: small correction — 60 qps sustained over 24h is 5.18M requests/day, yes — but your peak 250 qps is transient. for modeling we'll use sustained 60 qps. so tokens/day = 5.18M * 320 = ~1.66B tokens/day, that's huge — i think you meant 60 qps peak for a microservice, maybe daily average is 6-8 qps?
10:15 Rajiv Menon: oh right, typo — sustained is 6-8 qps, not 60. our daily average for this feature is about 7 qps. sorry.
10:38 Lucas Patel: that makes more sense. at 7 qps -> ~604k requests/day -> tokens/day ~193M.
11:05 Maya Chen: ok so 193M tokens/day. now per-token cost varies by model; for a high-quality open model we might estimate $0.0000008 per token on hosted after batching/caching assumptions — that's 0.8 microdollars per token — is that a fair starter?
11:45 Alyssa Greene: mm can you pause — that number seems small. can you show how that maps to monthly?
12:05 Lucas Patel: sure. at 193M tokens/day -> ~5.8B tokens/month. at $0.0000008 per token -> $4,640/month. but again that depends on model choice and how many output tokens are charged. also embeddings or reranks are separate.
12:50 Tom Brooks: that monthly number seems low relative to our expectation — are we sure about units?
13:20 Maya Chen: it's easy to get lost in zeros. breakdown: per-token price examples we gave: 0.8 microdollars/token (open quantized runtime) up to 3-4 microdollars/token for larger Llama-like variants on hosted. so the range matters a lot.
14:00 Rajiv Menon: ok, say we budget $50k/month — how close does that get us?
14:25 Lucas Patel: if we target $50k/month and you have 5.8B tokens/month, that implies ~0.0086 cents per token? let me reframe: $50k / 5.8B = $0.0000086 per token which is 8.6 microdollars. so you'd be well within that budget with the earlier per-token estimates. again caching could reduce effective tokens.
15:10 Alyssa Greene: can you explain batching impact — how do request latency and batching trade off here?
15:45 Lucas Patel: batching increases throughput and reduces unit cost because the GPU kernel overhead is amortized. but it adds scheduling delay. our runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs: you set a p95 latency SLO and the router will limit batching to keep within the SLO. for dedicated you can use larger batch windows to lower cost if you accept slightly higher p95.
16:40 Tom Brooks: so for our p95 400ms SLO, what batch sizes are realistic?
17:05 Lucas Patel: rough rule: for short sequences (<512 tokens) you can batch 4-8 and keep p95 under 400ms on modern A100/H100-ish equivalents. if you go to 16+ batching you'll see p95 go up; dedicated clusters with predictable load let you push batching more aggressively.
17:50 Rajiv Menon: what about autoscale and burst? we can't overspend if traffic spikes.
18:20 Maya Chen: you can set autoscale caps and burst buffers; we also have fallback policies to cheaper model variants that trigger when capacity is limited. cost throttles can be enforced by quotas.
19:05 Alyssa Greene: security question — we require SOC2 and SSO, and customer-managed KMS for keys. how does Redwood handle that in hosted?
19:40 Erin Soto: hosted supports BYOK via KMS integrations and we have SOC2 Type II and ISO docs we can share. for stricter controls we can run an early dedicated/VPC pilot where you manage the VPC and KMS.
20:20 Tom Brooks: do you provide audit logs per token/request for compliance?
20:45 Erin Soto: yes we provide request-level logs, RBAC, and retention policies configurable per account/route. we'll need to confirm exact retention limits for the pilot.
21:20 Rajiv Menon: for benching we want p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost/tk reported. can you propose measurement matrix?
21:50 Lucas Patel: yes — matrix: requests/sec, tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, GPU util, effective token billed (post-cache), and cost/tk. we'll also run quality spot checks (BLEU/ROUGE/LLM evals) for quantized variants.
22:30 Alyssa Greene: timeline? we want to start pilot in feb if possible.
22:55 Maya Chen: proposed timeline: this week (by 2027-01-03) we send pricing worksheet and data template; week of 2027-01-10 run bench (24-72h) in hosted sandbox with your prompt set; week of 2027-01-17 analyze results and decide hosted vs dedicated; target pilot kickoff 2027-02-01.
23:40 Tom Brooks: that timeline works for us assuming the bench shows acceptable latency.
24:10 Rajiv Menon: about the bench — what infra will you run on? cloud GPUs? we need details to ensure apples-to-apples.
24:40 Lucas Patel: for hosted bench we'll use our verified performance profiles on GPU types approximating H100/A100 depending on model. we'll record exact instance types and kernel versions; if you need exact parity we can run a dedicated bench in a VPC with your cloud account.
25:20 Alyssa Greene: cost modeling — can you show an extreme case where we hit 250 qps peak and how budget reacts?
25:50 Lucas Patel: yes — worst-case: 250 qps sustained -> 21.6M req/day -> tokens/day at 320 tokens = ~6.9B tokens/day which explodes cost; but that's unlikely and we can apply rate limits, queues, or cheap model fallbacks.
26:35 Tom Brooks: we will enforce rate limits but want graceful degradation not errors. fallback to smaller model is acceptable if quality is still OK.
27:10 Maya Chen: correct — Redwood router supports model variant fallbacks and region-based routing.
27:45 Rajiv Menon: can we get an initial pilot price estimate if we assume 7 qps avg, 120/200 token mix, and 30% caching hit?
28:10 Lucas Patel: quick calc: base tokens/day ~193M, with 30% cached effective billed tokens ~135M/day -> monthly ~4.05B tokens. at 1 microdollar/token that's ~$4k/month. at 4 microdollars/token ~$16k/month. both under your $50k/month target. add overhead for dedicated reserved capacity (~$10-20k/month) if you choose that route.
29:05 Alyssa Greene: ok that range is helpful. please put these scenarios in the pricing worksheet.
29:30 Maya Chen: will do. we'll include hosted per-token scenarios, dedicated reserved pricing, and a model of caching/batching impact.
30:10 Tom Brooks: on compliance — our security team will want the SOC2 and also a data flow diagram. can you include that?
30:35 Erin Soto: yes we'll include SOC2, ISO, data flow, and KMS notes with the security pack.
31:00 Rajiv Menon: any red flags about integrating with our auth? we use SAML SSO and internal RBAC.
31:25 Erin Soto: we support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC; for private deployments we can integrate with your IdP directly.
31:50 Alyssa Greene: ok great. on the bench results, what SLA for Redwood to run and deliver analysis? two business days after bench completion?
32:10 Lucas Patel: two business days is fine for the initial analysis. extended profiling may take longer.
32:40 Tom Brooks: what about data residency? some users are EU-only.
33:05 Maya Chen: hosted has regional deployments and can pin traffic to EU regions; for strict residency we recommend private deployment.
33:30 Rajiv Menon: one more technical — how do you measure effective tokens billed when we use partial KV cache hits and streaming?
33:55 Lucas Patel: the billing measure is based on decoded/generated tokens that traverse the model; prefix hits that bypass decode are not billed as full tokens. streaming doesn't change billing semantics, but partial streaming can increase overhead; we'll define exact counting in the benchmark script so it's reproducible.
34:40 Alyssa Greene: quality regressions are a big worry — can you run canary A/Bs on quantized variants during bench?
35:05 Lucas Patel: yes — we can run A/B canaries and guardrails; Redwood Optimize can track eval sets and trigger alerts if quality drops beyond threshold.
35:45 Rajiv Menon: ok, last question — are there any hidden costs like storage, network egress, or audit log charges?
36:10 Erin Soto: network egress is billed per cloud provider; audit log retention beyond the standard window may have charges. we'll flag estimated storage and egress in the worksheet.
36:55 Tom Brooks: sounds good. shall we summarize next steps?
37:20 Maya Chen: recap: Lucas to prepare benchmark plan + measurement matrix (due 2027-01-07). Maya to send pricing worksheet and data template (due 2027-01-03). Rajiv to share prompt set and test data access (due 2027-01-05). Redwood to schedule bench week of 2027-01-10.
38:05 Rajiv Menon: confirmed.
38:25 Alyssa Greene: confirmed.
38:40 Maya Chen: any competitors you're evaluating?
39:00 Tom Brooks: we are looking at Anthropic for hosted and some teams are testing OpenAI. also an internal self-host option.
39:25 Lucas Patel: understood — we'll highlight known tradeoffs: latency, unit cost, and private deployment complexity.
39:55 Rajiv Menon: quick wrinkle — our legal team will want a DPA and standard terms; can we get an initial template?
40:20 Erin Soto: yes we'll include DPA and standard terms in the packet.
40:45 Maya Chen: ok, any other questions?
41:00 Alyssa Greene: not from me.
41:10 Tom Brooks: no.
41:20 Rajiv Menon: no, thanks — excited to see the bench.
41:40 Maya Chen: great — we'll get materials out by next week. thanks all.
42:00 End of recorded transcript.

Notes: Transcript is auto-generated; occasional mis-transcriptions likely (product names: Redwood Dedicated sometimes shows as Redwood Dedicate).
